planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; GoldRush ripens very late and benefits from as much hang time as the season allows, developing its full rich, spicy-sweet flavor and honeyed texture only after several weeks in storage.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Released in 1994 from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois breeding program, GoldRush carries genetic immunity to apple scab along with strong resistance to fire blight and cedar-apple rust, making it one of the most reliable choices for growers who want to avoid a heavy fungicide program. The yellow-green, russeted fruit is quite tart and firm at harvest in October but mellows over weeks of cold storage into a dense, complex, honey-sweet apple that keeps for months, rivaling many classic long-keeping heirlooms. Pick late and store cool for the best eating quality.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Enterprise ripens in October, later than most main-season apples, and its disease-resistant genetics mean it needs little or no fungicide spraying in most home gardens.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Also from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding program and released in the early 1990s, Enterprise is immune to apple scab and resists fire blight and cedar-apple rust, making it a strong choice for low-spray or organic orchards. The medium-large, dark red fruit is crisp, firm, and sweet-tart with flavor that holds up well and even improves somewhat in storage. It ripens late in the season and keeps for several months under cool conditions.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Pristine ripens in midsummer, among the earliest disease-resistant apples available, well ahead of Enterprise and GoldRush from the same breeding program.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Released from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois program, Pristine is immune to apple scab and shows good resistance to fire blight and powdery mildew, making it a dependable low-spray choice for an early crop. The clear yellow, medium-sized fruit has crisp, juicy, mildly sweet-tart flesh best enjoyed fresh soon after picking, since it does not store as long as the program's later-season siblings. Its early ripening extends the home orchard's harvest window well before fall apples come in.

common_name: William's Pride Apple (Very Early Disease-Resistant Dark Red Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; William's Pride ripens in midsummer, among the very earliest apples of any kind, and fruit should be picked promptly since it softens quickly once ripe.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Also a product of the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding effort, William's Pride carries genetic immunity to apple scab along with resistance to fire blight, cedar-apple rust, and powdery mildew. The dark red, medium fruit ripens unusually early, often before the Fourth of July in warmer growing areas, with crisp, aromatic, mildly tart flesh. Because it softens fast after ripening, plan to harvest over a short window and use the fruit fresh rather than storing it.

common_name: Ashmead's Kernel Apple (English Heirloom Sharp-Flavored Russet Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Ashmead's Kernel is a light, biennial-prone bearer, so thin fruit in heavy years to encourage more even annual cropping.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Raised from seed around 1700 by Dr. William Ashmead of Gloucester, England, this is one of the oldest russet apples still grown and is treasured by cider makers and flavor enthusiasts for its intense, sharp, pear-drop sweetness balanced against high acidity. The medium, dull green-gold fruit is entirely covered in rough russet skin and looks unassuming, but the dense, dry, richly flavored flesh has made it a favorite of English apple connoisseurs for centuries. It ripens in mid-fall and its flavor improves somewhat with a few weeks of storage.
